**Patient Vignette: Mrs. A.**

Mrs. A. is a 74-year-old woman who presents to the clinic at the urging of her partner, Samuel. She has been living with him for the past twelve years on a small farm in a rural area, where she continues to work as an agricultural laborer. She is a tall, dignified woman with deeply calloused hands and a quiet, watchful stillness. She speaks softly, often pausing to look down at her lap, and she apologizes three times during the first session for "wasting my time."

The story she tells begins not in the present, but forty years ago, in her home country in West Africa. She was 34, a mother of two young children, and she worked as a street vendor selling vegetables. One evening, walking home along a dirt path through a field, a man she recognized from the market pulled her into the tall grass. He held a knife to her throat. "He told me if I screamed, he would find my children," she says, her voice flat. "So I did not scream."

She did not tell anyone for thirty-eight years. Not her husband at the time, not her sisters, not the village elders. In her culture, she explains, a woman who is raped is often seen as spoiled, as having brought shame upon her family. "I thought it was my fault," she says. "I should have walked a different way. I should have run faster." She buried the memory, she says, the way she buries rotten fruit in the compost—deep enough so no one can see it, but knowing it is still there, breaking down beneath the surface.

For decades, she functioned. She raised her children, she cooked, she worked in the fields. But she describes a life lived in a state of low-grade dread. She never walked alone after dark. She never let her children out of her sight. She developed a habit of always sitting with her back to a wall, a practice she continues to this day.

The trauma broke open three years ago, when her eldest granddaughter turned 16. Mrs. A. saw the girl laughing with a young man at a family gathering, and the memory of the dirt path, the knife, the smell of the grass, came back with a force that knocked her to her knees. She began having nightmares—not of the rape itself, but of a sensation of being pinned down, unable to breathe, with a heavy weight on her chest. She wakes up gasping, convinced she is back in that field.

Her work has become a minefield. She is a gifted farmer, known for her ability to coax tomatoes from stubborn soil. But now, the act of bending over in the rows of crops triggers a visceral panic. The feeling of the sun on the back of her neck, the smell of damp earth, the sound of rustling leaves—all of it sends her heart racing. She has taken to working only in the early mornings, before the sun is high, and she refuses to work in any field that borders a road. Samuel has had to take over the weeding, a task she once loved.

She is hypervigilant in a way that exhausts her. She checks the locks on the door seven times before bed. She cannot tolerate Samuel touching her from behind, even gently. When he reached for her shoulder in the kitchen last week to ask her a question, she spun around and threw a cup at the wall. She was so ashamed she did not speak to him for two days. "He is a good man," she whispers. "But I am a broken woman. I am too old to be this scared."

Her PCL-5 score of 65 reflects the severity of her symptoms: the intrusive memories, the avoidance of any reminder of the assault, the negative beliefs about herself as damaged and weak, and the constant, vibrating state of arousal. She has not told Samuel the full story. She has only said that "something bad happened." She came to the clinic today because she is terrified she is losing her mind, and because she wants to be able to walk to the mailbox without feeling like she is about to die. She looks at me with a mixture of hope and deep suspicion. "Can you take this out of me?" she asks. "Can you make me forget?"
